headline: Tonight's rain mostly misses New York City, but a much bigger storm late Wednesday night through Friday brings 1–2 inches of rain, strong east-northeast winds gusting 35–45 mph and widespread coastal flooding on Thanksgiving.

sections.title: Today & Tonight
sections.text: Low pressure now looks to pass just east of Long Island Sunday night, so rain totals were cut sharply: little to none for New York City and areas north and west, while far eastern Long Island and southeast Connecticut get 0.75 to 1 inch of moderate to locally heavy rain. A little light rain could still fall west of the main rain band. The rain falls mainly this evening into the early morning hours Monday, and with the storm's more eastward track, winds will be much weaker than earlier expected.

sections.title: Short Term
sections.text: Any leftover rain exits eastern areas Monday morning, skies clear, and a cold front passes in the afternoon with northwest gusts around 20 mph; Monday is another warm day in the 60s, though record highs near 70 are unlikely to fall (Islip has tied or broken its record high each of the last four days). Much colder air arrives Tuesday and Wednesday under an unusually strong area of high pressure to the north: highs struggle to get out of the 40s, and lows drop mainly below freezing, except in the New York City metro area Wednesday morning.

sections.title: Long Term
sections.text: A much larger storm brings potentially significant impacts from late Wednesday night into Friday, with a broad band of rain stretching from the Ohio Valley to the Atlantic coast, so escaping bad weather for Thanksgiving is unlikely. East-northeast winds build Wednesday into Thursday, peaking during the day Thursday at 20–30 mph with gusts of 35–45 mph, possibly 50 mph at the coast. Rain totals of 1–2 inches look reasonable, and the storm is carrying a lot of moisture thanks to a strong southern jet stream tied to El Niño. Some computer models track the low farther west along the Appalachians, but strong winds are expected either way; rain chances linger mainly Friday morning, with west winds gusting around 30–35 mph.

coast: A minimal coastal flood threat exists at most for the south shore back bays of Nassau County and Queens during Monday morning's high tide, and water levels will likely fall just short of minor flooding, so no Coastal Flood Statement is planned. Thursday is a much bigger concern: with a full moon on the 24th and king tides this week, many spots need less than a foot of extra water to reach minor flooding, and the current forecast supports widespread minor to moderate coastal flooding, perhaps even localized major flooding, along with beach flooding, erosion and overwash. On the water, gale warnings for the outer ocean waters were dropped; Small Craft Advisories remain for the nearshore ocean waters until 6 AM Tuesday and for Long Island Sound east of the Connecticut River until 6 PM Monday. After a possible brief lull Tuesday afternoon and night, east-northeast winds ramp up Wednesday, reaching gale force on the ocean Wednesday night and storm force Thursday, with gales on the Sound and bays late Wednesday night into Thursday; peak waves reach 15–20 feet on the ocean (20–25 feet out east), 7–10 feet on Long Island Sound and around 10 feet on western Block Island Sound.
watch_for: Widespread minor to moderate, possibly localized major, coastal flooding on Thursday with king tides and the full moon.
Strong east-northeast winds Thursday, gusting 35–45 mph and possibly 50 mph at the coast.
The storm's track: a path farther west along the Appalachians would change rain and wind details.
confidence: Forecasters are fairly confident tonight's rain stays mainly east of New York City and that a cold Tuesday and Wednesday follow, while a significant Thanksgiving storm looks likely but the exact extent of its rain, wind and coastal flooding impacts is still uncertain.
